problems.1: Adding data makes some estimates less certain
problems.2: Machinery output does not match official industrial production
problems.3: Oil and gas totals are confident, pinned down by data, and wrong
problems.4: Inventory and shipment data are fitted poorly even after being seen
problems.5: The ranges on sector totals are too narrow
problems.7: The assumed noise in most observations is set too high
problems.8: The headline forecast check partly measures the model against itself
problems.9: Some parameters rest mainly on their priors
problems.10: Retail demand is unsettled and has the largest forecast errors

fixes.label: 1A
fixes.title: Let observations move only what they measure
fixes.fix: Let each kind of observation move only the quantities it measures or directly drives. Today a sector-wide statistic can nudge every quantity in the sector, including finished stock, which has no pull back toward a normal level, so accidental nudges pile up and push the copies of the world apart. Limiting finished stock to inventory observations should stop that buildup.
fixes.test: Filter this world's four run dates again from the existing fits with and without the change; Machinery's finished inventory (177) and Semiconductors' (8.34) spread ratios should fall below 1.2, and no other ratio should rise.

fixes.label: 1B
fixes.title: Compute the spread ratio from average spreads
fixes.fix: Check the measure before trusting its largest values. The spread ratio averages month-by-month ratios, so a few months where the copies without data barely differ can alone produce a value like 177; a ratio of average spreads, over months that are truly uncertain, would show which sectors are really unsettled. This corrects the reading, not the filter.
fixes.test: Recompute the spread ratios for this run both ways; the count of ratios above 1.2 and the extreme values (177, 10.9, 8.34) should drop where they came from a few nearly certain months.

fixes.label: 1C
fixes.title: Run the filter with 400 copies instead of 100
fixes.fix: Run the filter with about four times as many copies of the world (400 instead of 100). With few copies, chance agreements between unrelated quantities look like real links and the filter acts on them; more copies shrink those accidents. In an earlier test of one sector's inventory fit, more copies reduced a similar problem but did not remove it, so this is a supporting step rather than a cure.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits at all four run dates with 400 copies; the spread ratios above 1.2 should fall toward 1, most of all for New orders in Housing (4.84) and Data centers (2.74).

fixes.label: 1D
fixes.title: Drop the random jitter for sector-wide statistics
fixes.fix: Update the copies of the world for sector-wide statistics without the random jitter that the current method adds to the observation for each copy. That jitter keeps the spread right on average for the quantity being observed, but when one sector total pulls on hundreds of quantities at once, it mostly adds noise to the quantities the statistic says little about.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits at the four run dates with the jitter-free update for sector-wide statistics only; spread ratios above 1.2 in Machinery and Retail should fall while the agreement with official statistics stays the same or improves.

fixes.label: 2A
fixes.title: Tie Machinery's untracked part to official production
fixes.fix: Tie the overall size of Machinery's untracked part of the industry to the official production index during the fit, as most other sectors already do. Nothing else makes it add up to the official total, and the tracked companies are known to be atypical. On an earlier test world this made Machinery's error slightly worse (5.6% to 7.9%), so judge accuracy too.
fixes.test: Refit Machinery at all four run dates on this world and on one other seed; industrial production should move from 26/100 with a 13.4% gap toward 90/100 with a gap of a few percent, without the forecast gap rising.

fixes.label: 2B
fixes.title: Let the filter adjust Machinery's lasting level
fixes.fix: Let the filter adjust a lasting level for the sector (the size of the untracked part) when official production disagrees, instead of only pushing on single months. Those pushes are undone by the model's dynamics the next month, leaving a steady gap and spreading the copies apart (Output ratio 10.9). Adjusting semiconductors' order level this way steadied that sector in every test.
fixes.test: Filter the existing Machinery and Oil and gas fits at all four run dates with the level adjustable; the industrial production gap (13.4%) and the Output spread ratio (10.9) should both fall.

fixes.label: 2C
fixes.title: Pool Machinery's untracked part less with tracked firms
fixes.fix: Pool the untracked machinery entities' behavior less strongly with the tracked companies'. Earlier work found that the tracked machinery companies keep shorter normal lead times than the rest of the industry, and the fit pulls the untracked part toward them, which sets its order book and output level wrong; a separate group average for the untracked part would let the industry-wide data on unfilled orders set it instead.
fixes.test: Refit Machinery at all four run dates with the separate group; the industrial production gap should shrink and the industry unfilled-orders observations should fit at least as well.

fixes.label: 3A
fixes.title: Tie oil and gas's untracked part to official production
fixes.fix: Tie the overall size of oil and gas's untracked part to the official production index during the fit, as most other sectors do. Nothing else makes it add up to the official figure, leaving a steady 3% gap. The tie was turned off after it hurt one run date on an earlier world, and the model has changed since, so the odds are even.
fixes.test: Refit Oil and gas at all four run dates on this world and one other seed; industrial production should rise from 4/100 and utilization from 51/100, with no run date's forecast gap growing.

fixes.label: 3B
fixes.title: Let the filter adjust oil and gas's lasting level
fixes.fix: Let the filter adjust a lasting level for oil and gas output when the official index disagrees, rather than reshaping each month's random shocks. Earlier, forcing oil's total toward the official figure month by month emptied its finished stock, because the monthly pushes had to come from somewhere; a lasting level moves the total without distorting stocks.
fixes.test: Filter the existing Oil and gas fits at the four run dates with the adjustable level; the 3.2% production gap should shrink and finished stock should stay in line with the stock observations.

fixes.label: 3C
fixes.title: Refit oil and gas without industry-wide stock data
fixes.fix: Refit oil and gas without the industry-wide stock observations to see whether they are what pulls output away from the official index. Those stock figures once drove oil's stocks to zero and stalled its shipments; if dropping them closes the gap, the way they link stock to production needs work before they are used again.
fixes.test: Refit Oil and gas at all four run dates with and without the stock observations; compare the industrial production gap (3.2%) and the observation fit of the stock figures.

fixes.label: 3D
fixes.title: Make official statistics bind tighter for oil and gas
fixes.fix: Make the official statistics bind more tightly for oil and gas by shrinking the extra allowance the filter grants because the official figure already contains the tracked producers' data (now 1.5 times the base allowance). A smaller allowance pulls the total harder toward the official figure. Past experience warns that a harder pull through monthly shocks can distort stocks, so this should follow the lasting-level fix rather than replace it.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits at the four run dates with the smaller allowance; industrial production should rise above 4/100 while oil's finished-stock observations still fit.

fixes.label: 4A
fixes.title: Stop unrelated observations from moving finished stock
fixes.fix: Stop observations that are not about inventories from moving finished stock. Finished stock has no pull back toward a normal level, so every small accidental nudge from an unrelated observation stays in it; the finished-inventory observations come in below the model's prediction on average (by about 0.7 of a standard deviation, before being used), which fits stocks that have drifted upward that way.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits at the four run dates with the change; finished inventory should move from 80/100 toward 90/100 and its average surprise toward zero.

fixes.label: 4B
fixes.title: Let industry inventories adjust the normal stock level
fixes.fix: Let the industry-wide inventory figures (the sector inventories, 94 monthly observations) adjust the untracked entities' normal stock level, not only this month's stock. Those figures are predicted well just before they are used (their surprises have about the expected size) but fit badly afterward, so the filter takes each one in and the model then drifts away again; a lasting level would keep the correction.
fixes.test: Filter wholesale at the four run dates with the adjustable stock level; sector inventories should move from 43/100 toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 4C
fixes.title: Shield finished stock from non-inventory observations
fixes.fix: Stop observations that are not about inventories from moving finished stock. Finished stock has no pull back toward a normal level, so every accidental nudge from an unrelated observation stays in it. The finished-inventory observations come in about 0.7 of a standard deviation below prediction before use, which fits stocks that have drifted upward that way.
fixes.test: Refit the sectors whose census shipments miss most, at all four run dates; census shipments should move from 78/100 toward 90/100 and their average surprise toward zero.

fixes.label: 5A
fixes.title: Count the filter's own allowance in the totals check
fixes.fix: When checking sector totals against official statistics, count the allowance the filter itself grants for the gap between its total and the official figure (about 1.5%), and the published band widening, not only the copies' disagreement. The check now uses a narrower range than the model publishes, so small gaps such as hotel employment's 1.3% count as misses.
fixes.test: Rebuild the official-statistics page for this run; the overall share inside the range should rise from 79/100 toward 90/100, with Machinery and Oil and gas still marked as disagreeing.

fixes.label: 5B
fixes.title: Add a shared sector-wide part to random shocks
fixes.fix: Give the copies of the world a shared, sector-wide part in their random shocks, so that a copy that runs high does so for most entities in the sector together. Today each entity's randomness is drawn on its own, so it largely cancels when entities are added up: ranges for single entities come out wide (problem 7) while ranges for sector totals come out narrow.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits at the four run dates with the shared part; the official-statistics share inside the range should rise toward 90/100 while observations of single entities stay near 90/100.

fixes.label: 5C
fixes.title: Set band widening per sector
fixes.fix: Set the widening of the published bands per sector rather than one factor for all sectors, calibrated on backtests of a different synthetic world. A single factor leaves sectors such as Hotels and Hospitals narrow while others are wider than needed.
fixes.test: Calibrate on the other world's four-date backtest and apply to this run; Hotels' forecast coverage should rise from 84/100 and the share of official months inside the range toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 6A
fixes.title: Set forecast band widening per quantity
fixes.fix: Set the widening of forecast bands per quantity, calibrated on backtests of a different synthetic world, so that capacity and capacity in use get more widening and well-pinned quantities less. One factor per status cannot fit both: overall the forecasts are wider than needed, while capacity is too narrow.
fixes.test: Apply per-quantity factors from the other world's backtest to this run's forecasts; Capacity in use should rise from 67/100 and Capacity from 81/100 toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 6B
fixes.title: Let capacity growth rates wander over time
fixes.fix: Let each entity's capacity growth rate wander slowly over time in the copies of the world, instead of holding one value for the whole window and forecast. A fixed rate makes a year-ahead capacity range nearly as narrow as today's, while real growth speeds up and slows down. It needs a refit and changes the model, so the odds are even.
fixes.test: Run full four-date backtests on this world and one other seed; Capacity forecast coverage should rise from 81/100 toward 90/100 without the forecast gap growing.

fixes.label: 7A
fixes.title: Score observations before the model uses them
fixes.fix: Score observations against the model's prediction just before each observation is used, not after. The filter already records these surprises, and for most kinds their size is close to what the stated noise implies (about 0.75 to 0.95 of the expected spread), so much of the "wider than needed" verdict comes from scoring data the model has already absorbed.
fixes.test: Rebuild the observations page from the recorded surprises; the typical observation should sit near 41% of the way to the edge for most kinds, separating real over-width from the effect of in-sample scoring.

fixes.label: 7B
fixes.title: Narrow the spread of each entity's parameters
fixes.fix: Narrow the spread of parameters that the copies of the world draw for each entity. That spread includes an extra term for the fit's own random-number noise and is capped only at the prior range, which makes single-entity predictions wider than the data need. This must be weighed against problem 5, since narrower entity ranges also narrow sector totals unless the shared sector-wide part is added.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits at the four run dates with the narrower draws; observations should move from 95/100 toward 90/100, and sector-total coverage should be watched for a drop.

fixes.label: 7C
fixes.title: Widen bands less for well-pinned quantities
fixes.fix: Use less widening on forecast bands for quantities the data pin down. The widening was calibrated against the truth, where the model's own biases count; against its own later estimates, which share those biases, the same widening looks too generous for well-observed quantities.
fixes.test: Apply smaller factors to quantities with spread ratios below 0.5; forecast coverage against later estimates should move from 96/100 toward 90/100 for Chemicals, Housing, Steel and Wholesale.

fixes.label: 7D
fixes.title: Lower each observation's assumed noise
fixes.fix: Lower the assumed noise of each kind of observation until its surprises have the expected size. In this synthetic world the data are generated with exactly the assumed noise, so the extra width comes from the copies of the world, not from the noise; lowering the noise would make the check look better while giving the data too much weight.
fixes.test: Filter the existing fits with the lowered noise; observations would move toward 90/100, but forecast gaps should be checked for a rise.

fixes.label: 8A
fixes.title: Leave model-driven quantities out of the headline check
fixes.fix: Report the headline forecast check separately for quantities the data pin down and quantities that come mostly from the model's equations (spread ratio 0.8 or above), and leave the second group out of the headline. Where nothing observes a quantity, the forecast and the later estimate come from the same equations and agree whether or not they are right.
fixes.test: Rebuild the forecast page; the headline should no longer include Input inventory, the model-driven New orders, Overdue and Phantom orders, and should show a lower share inside the range or a larger gap.

fixes.label: 8B
fixes.title: Check forecasts against observations not yet used
fixes.fix: Add a check of forecasts against observations published after the forecast date, before the model has used them. Unlike later estimates, these come from outside the model, so they show forecast accuracy and range width without the model scoring itself.
fixes.test: Filter the earlier run dates again, saving each forecast's predicted observations, and score them against the observations published later; a new table of forecast misses against fresh data should appear.

fixes.label: 8C
fixes.title: Show a simple baseline beside each forecast score
fixes.fix: Show a simple baseline next to each forecast score, such as carrying the last estimate forward or repeating last year's seasonal pattern. A perfect score that the baseline also reaches says nothing about the model; a score that beats it does.
fixes.test: Rebuild the forecast page with the baseline beside each quantity; quantities where the model does no better than the baseline (likely Overdue orders, Phantom orders and Lost demand) should be marked.

fixes.label: 9A
fixes.title: Estimate emissions slope and markup once per sector
fixes.fix: Estimate the emissions slope and the starting markup once per sector instead of once per entity, in the sectors where that predicts held-back observations better. Earlier tests of moving parameters to one value per sector helped Food and Machinery and hurt Steel, so the choice has to be made sector by sector on held-back data, not across the board.
fixes.test: Hold back a fifth of the observations at two run dates in the sectors with emissions data, fit both ways, and keep the version with the better held-out score; the count of entity parameters resting on their priors should drop.

fixes.label: 9B
fixes.title: Stop estimating biases the data cannot separate
fixes.fix: Stop estimating per entity the observation biases that no other data can separate from the quantity they bias, such as semiconductors' lead-time bias (0% informative) and the list-price gap; hold them at their assumed values or share one value per sector. Earlier tests found that observation parameters like these barely affect accuracy, so little is lost.
fixes.test: Refit Semiconductors and the sectors with list prices at all four run dates; those parameters should leave the uninformative list and the forecast gaps should not rise.

fixes.label: 9C
fixes.title: Add data that varies the way parameters need
fixes.fix: Add data that varies in the way these parameters need, such as monthly plant emissions for heavy emitters (which separate the emissions slope from its intercept) and more frequent stated capacity (which pins down capacity drift). This needs a new synthetic world and, on real data, sources that publish at that frequency.
fixes.test: Build a world with the added observations and run a full four-date backtest; the emissions slope and capacity drift should be informative for clearly more than half of their entities.

fixes.label: 10A
fixes.title: Let the filter adjust Retail's lasting demand level
fixes.fix: Let the filter adjust retail's lasting demand level, as it already does for semiconductors' order level, instead of only reshaping each month's shocks. Each monthly correction toward official retail sales is undone by the model's dynamics, which spreads the copies apart (New orders 2.27). Retail's load factor itself is legitimate: the share of goods on offer that sell.
fixes.test: Filter the existing retail fits at the four run dates with the adjustable level; retail's spread ratios should fall below 1.2 and its 4.6% forecast gap should shrink.

fixes.label: 10B
fixes.title: Give Retail a stronger parameter search
fixes.fix: Give retail's fit the stronger search settings that oil and gas and wholesale already use (more steps per round and more rounds). In earlier tests retail's fit stopped further short of the best parameters than any other sector's, and the two sectors given their own settings both improved.
fixes.test: Refit retail at all four run dates on this world and one other seed; the 4.6% forecast gap should fall without the observation fit getting worse.

fixes.label: 10C
fixes.title: Update Retail in smaller steps each month
fixes.fix: Update retail in more, smaller steps each month. Retail can only sell what it has on hand, so copies of the world near that limit react in opposite ways to the same sales figure, and one large step pushes them apart; several smaller steps follow the limit more closely, as the existing two-step update does in milder form.
fixes.test: Filter the existing retail fits at the four run dates with four steps instead of two; retail's spread ratios above 1.2 should fall.
